target: AG1’s claim that making Election Day a national holiday would remove the main voting barrier created by work and school schedules.
objection: A federal holiday would not guarantee paid time off from private employers, so many low-wage retail, food service, health support, and gig workers would still have to work. That means the holiday could leave the most schedule-constrained workers facing the same barrier, just with holiday branding instead of real access.

target: AG1’s implication that a national holiday would be broadly beneficial and fair to everyone.
objection: A holiday could create new inequities because people whose employers offer time off would benefit, while workers at employers that do not offer meaningful leave—often the people most likely to need it—would not.

target: AG1’s suggestion that a holiday is the right central reform compared with other voting reforms.
objection: Direct voting-access reforms such as mandatory time off to vote, automatic voter registration, and easier ID/registration rules are more reliable because they change voting logistics directly instead of depending on a holiday.

target: AG1’s claim that an election-day holiday meaningfully increases turnout by itself.
objection: Research and past experience indicate that an election-day holiday alone is usually not as effective at increasing turnout as targeted voting-access reforms.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would be merely symbolic and leave workers exposed.
objection: The holiday is meant to create a broad default in which schools and many workplaces are closed or reduced, so most people are not forced to choose between voting and earning wages; it can also be paired with enforceable time-to-vote or paid-leave protections rather than replacing them.

target: AG1’s rebuttal that the holiday can be paired with workplace protections and therefore solves the problem.
objection: If the real fix is enforceable workplace protections, then the holiday is redundant at best and politically distracting at worst, because the holiday alone still would not guarantee paid leave for private-employer workers and retail/service jobs often would not shut down.

target: AG1’s use of OECD countries as evidence for the holiday.
objection: The OECD comparison is not comparable to the U.S. because countries that hold elections on holidays often also have broader labor protections and different paid-leave regimes; without enforceable U.S. employer-time mandates, the workers with the least flexible schedules still benefit least.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday is not meant to be the only policy and can still fix schedule conflicts.
objection: Relying on a day off is an indirect solution: school closure does not solve the core issue for many low-income workers, whose employers still control their hours and whose wages are still lost unless there are targeted, enforceable time-to-vote or paid-leave rules.

target: AG1’s proposal to bundle the holiday with workplace protections.
objection: Bundling the holiday with workplace protections creates political and implementation risk because the holiday can become the headline while the enforcement of those protections gets weakened, leaving low-income workers behind.

target: AG1’s claim that a nationwide holiday would spread voting across the day and reduce pressure.
objection: A universal holiday can concentrate voting demand into the same day and create longer lines, which hurts inflexible, low-income workers who cannot easily wait or return multiple times.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would create longer lines and peak demand.
objection: A holiday does not force everyone to vote at the same moment; by removing work and school conflicts, it lets people vote at more hours across the day, and election administrators can plan staffing and polling capacity around a fixed day off.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reduces the after-work/before-school crunch and improves capacity.
objection: The central problem for low-income workers is not just timing but income security and employer control; many hourly or contract workers will still be scheduled or undercompensated unless there are enforceable time-to-vote or paid-leave rules.

target: AG1’s suggestion that adding workplace protections to the holiday makes it worthwhile.
objection: If the holiday must be paired with the same workplace protections and voting-logistics reforms that could be enacted without a holiday, then the holiday adds risk and political distraction without being a reliable turnout driver on its own.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is only a calendar convenience and does not help voting operations.
objection: Election Day as a national holiday also helps with where voting happens and who can support it, because polling sites often rely on schools and other public facilities; a holiday makes those locations easier to keep available and operate smoothly.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday improves polling-site availability and election administration.
objection: That is an election-administration argument, not a worker-access argument; polling-site capacity can be funded directly through staffing and facility arrangements without making Election Day a holiday that still does not ensure paid time off for many low-income workers.

target: AG1’s broader defense that a holiday helps low-income people by fitting voting into family routines and community planning.
objection: For low-income families, school closures can create new burdens such as needing childcare or supervision, while hourly and essential workers still face employer-controlled schedules and possible wage loss, so the holiday can simply shift the burden rather than remove it.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday meaningfully broadens participation through shared civic culture.
objection: Without enforceable paid-leave/time-to-vote rules and demand-spreading reforms like early voting, mail voting, and streamlined registration, a national holiday can widen inequality instead of closing the voting-access gap.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday improves system capacity by enabling more poll workers and locations.
objection: The holiday does not solve the main problem of whether workers can vote without losing income or control of their schedules; targeted reforms are more reliable, and the holiday alone has not been shown to be an effective turnout strategy.
